source: BNBC 2020 Part 6 Chapter 3: site investigation, identification of problem soils, soil chemistry for buried steel and concrete; Chapter 5 Sec 5.5: concrete in the ground

borings.note: The code names 'small buildings' and 'large' (count) or 'multistoried' (spacing) buildings without a limit between them: the engineer picks the size, and SAEngine reads 'large' and 'multistoried' as one. The 67 % inside the building is the rule of Sec 3.4.4(ix) for large areas; for one building (viii) asks for the borings near the foundations, so a shortfall is a warning.

sources.spread: Sec 3.4.5(i): below the bearing level, 2 footing widths where L <= 2B, 4 widths where L >= 5B, linear between (L/B, depth in widths)
sources.minimum: Sec 3.4.5(vii): never less than 2 m (the depth weathering reaches, where deeper)
sources.buildingWidthFactor: Sec 3.4.5(ii): multistoried and framed buildings: at least 50 % of the borings to 1.5 x the building width below the lowest part of the foundation
sources.belowPileTip: Sec 3.4.5(iv): at least 6 m below the pile or shaft tip; 2 x the largest group dimension below the tip for a group, unless end bearing on rock
sources.rockCore: Sec 3.4.5(v): piles on rock: at least 1.5 m of rock core at each boring
sources.shaftRockCoreDiameters: Sec 3.4.5(vi): shafts on or into rock: 1.5 m, 3 shaft diameters (isolated) or 2 x the group dimension, whichever is greater
sources.bedrockCore: Sec 3.4.5(viii): at least one boring to bedrock (cored 3 m into it) or well below the level of influence of the building

classes.label: little effect on behaviour; inorganic soil
affects the properties, behaves like a mineral soil: organic silts and clays
organic matter governs the properties: silty or clayey organic soil
behaviour distinct from traditional soil mechanics: peat

organic.clause: BNBC 2020 Part 6 Sec 3.5.4, Table 6.3.3 (p. 711); Table 6.3.2 OL/OH/PT (pp. 708-709)
organic.note: Table 6.3.3 prints whole-number bands (< 5, 6-20, 21-74, > 75 %). A value between bands takes the band below, except 5 %, which is not '< 5 %' and so counts as organic (the safer side).

criteria.source: Appendix E (5), IS 2911 Part 3, liquid limit
Appendix E (5), IS 2911 Part 3, plasticity index
Appendix E (8), Seed et al. (1962), air dry to saturated
Appendix E (9), Look (2007), PI x percent passing 425 um

expansive.clause: BNBC 2020 Part 6 Sec 3.5.5 and Appendix E (p. 711; part 2 pp. 451-453)
expansive.note: Appendix E prints overlapping bands (USBR, Seed, Chen): a value on a shared bound takes the more severe degree. Each criterion is read on its own and the most severe degree found is the sample's. The weighted plasticity index is PI times the percent passing 425 um (Look 2007), as the appendix describes it; its formula is not legible in the gazette.

sources.criticalVoidRatio: Eq 6.3.1: ec = 0.85 eL + 0.15 eP; collapse is probable when e0 > ec
sources.voidIndexMax: Eq 6.3.2: for Sr <= 0.6, collapsible when (eL - e0)/(1 + e0) <= 0.10
sources.relativeSubsidence: Eq 6.3.3: imc = (H - H')/H; collapsible when imc >= 0.02

collapsible.note: eL and eP are the void ratios at the liquid and plastic limits, w Gs (saturated). Eq 6.3.2 and the relation signs of Sr and imc are not legible in the text layer of the gazette; they were read from the equation glyphs and match the usual form of the criterion.

dispersive.note: ESP = Na/CEC x 100 and EMgP = Mg/CEC x 100, the exchangeable sodium and magnesium over the cation exchange capacity (meq/100 g); the numerators of Eqs 6.3.4-6.3.5 are not legible in the gazette. The code says dispersive soil does not trouble buildings itself (it matters for embankments and dams): the result is a note.

softClay.note: N is the field SPT blow count. The table prints N 2-4 for soft clay: N = 4 is taken as soft (the safer side).

sources.compositionFromUscs: SAEngine practice, not BNBC: the soil group when the composition is not entered (clean sand and gravel as 'non-stratified sand'; silts and silty or clayey sands as 'sandy silt, sandy clay, clayey silt'; clays; organic soils as 'peat, marshy soil')
sources.ratings: Table 6.3.6b: 0 and above non-corrosive, 0 to -4 slightly corrosive, -5 to -10 corrosive, -10 or less highly corrosive

corrosivity.note: Table 6.3.6b prints 0 in two bands (non-corrosive, slightly corrosive) and -10 in two (corrosive, highly corrosive): the more severe rating is used at both. On a shared bound of Table 6.3.6a the lower (more corrosive) score is used. A parameter not tested scores 0 and the rating says so.

steelCorrosion.note: mm per side per year. Recent fill and industrial waste can corrode faster: protection should be considered there.

corrosiveSite.note: ppm in the soil or the ground water: chloride >= 500, sulphate >= 2000 or pH < 6 makes the site corrosive for structural elements.

classes.name: Moderate
classes.cement: other than CEM I and B type

classes.name: Severe
classes.cement: other than CEM I and B type

classes.name: Very severe
classes.cement: other than CEM I and B type

sulphate.note: Water-soluble SO4 in the soil [% by weight] or in the water [ppm]. The bands share their bounds: 0.10 % / 150 ppm and 0.20 % / 1500 ppm take the more severe class; 'very severe' starts above 2.00 % / 10 000 ppm as printed. Sulphate-resisting cement with the class's water-cement ratio is the alternative Sec 5.5.2.1 allows; calcium chloride is not used in severe and very severe exposure (Sec 5.5.2.2). Sea water is moderate (Table 6.5.2 note 2).

sources.maxWaterCement: Sec 5.5.1.2: reinforced concrete exposed to brackish water, sea water or their spray: w/c <= 0.40, or 0.45 with the cover of Sec 8.1.8 increased by 12 mm
sources.lowPermeabilityWaterCement: Sec 5.5.1.1: concrete to have low permeability when exposed to water: w/c <= 0.50

chloride.note: SAEngine practice, not BNBC: ground whose chloride makes the site corrosive (Sec 3.10.1.29, >= 500 ppm) is treated as brackish for Sec 5.5.1.2, and concrete below the water table as exposed to water for Sec 5.5.1.1.

geoHazards.note: A preliminary review of the site for each hazard; a detailed analysis only where the review finds a significant threat.

liquefaction.note: The code obtains Eq 6.3.8 by dividing Eq 6.3.7a by the effective vertical stress, so its CSR carries no 0.65 factor (the peak stress ratio): on the safe side of the CRR curve calibrated against 0.65 tmax. CRR 'can be obtained by several procedures' and is most commonly taken from the SPT; the code prescribes none: Youd et al. (2001), SAEngine's choice. The rule of thumb is read with the field N as measured (Sec 3.9.5 does not say which N; the SPT value of the site classes, Sec 2.5.3.2, is the field N).

sources.clays: BNBC 3.9.5: clays do not liquefy except sensitive clays
sources.pga: BNBC 2020 Sec 2.5.13.2; Sec 2.5.3.1 asks for liquefaction under design earthquake ground motions
sources.zone: seismic zoning map: the maximum considered PGA on rock, Sec 2.5.4.2 and Table 6.2.14

siteClassification.note: N is the field blow count (uncorrected) and the means are harmonic (Eqs 6.2.31-6.2.33); nMax 100 is ASCE 7-16 20.4's cap, SAEngine practice. SA needs a measured shear wave velocity; SE needs the Vs of the alluvium and of the material below; S1's high water content is not checked.
